ROS/RNS, and in particular ROS produced by iron, can stimulate ryanodines receptors and thereby contribute to normal neuronal synaptic plasticity, whereas excessive production of ROS/RNS may contribute to neurotoxicity and neurodegeneration.

ROS/RNS species, including ROS generated via the Fenton reaction by iron, are necessary for normal synaptic plasticity, that the ryanodine calcium release channel may be the molecular link between ROS/RNS and the activation of the signaling pathways needed to induce gene transcription, and that excessive ROS production may contribute, at least in part, to neurodegeneration.

(1) ROS and RNS, including ROS produced by the Fenton reaction in the presence of iron, stimulate ryanoidine receptor-mediated calcium signaling; (2) calcium release stimulated by ROS and RNS activates the signaling cascades needed to induce synaptic plasticity and (3) too much iron and/or ROS production may lead to excessive calcium release, which in turn, may cause neurodegeneration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possible involvement of ROS/RNS and iron in synaptic plasticity and neurodegeneration.
the role that ROS/RNS and iron play in the normal function of the central nervous system, as well as in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases.
the physiological role of ROS/RNS and iron on neuronal functions, including synaptic plasticity.

calcium and ROS/RNs have a central role in the signaling cascades leading to synaptic plasticity and learning and memory, but that too much ROS production and iron accumulation may be deleterious to the brain.
ROS/RNS and iron play a role in neuronal synaptic plasticity and that their overproduction may be detrimental to the brain.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ROS/RNS and iron play a dual, but essential, role in neuronal function.

The main takeaway from our work is that
ROS, iron and calcium are tightly linked in the regulation of synaptic plasticity.
the generation of ROS and RNS, including those derived from iron, can be considered as a normal component of neuronal signaling cascades, and not only as a deleterious process.
